entry.title: Jamdar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1620
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted an extension of time but dismissed an appeal from the Administrative Review Tribunal, which had affirmed refusal of Australian citizenship by conferral on good-character grounds. The applicant challenged the Tribunal’s treatment of earlier non-conviction offending and its finding that he deliberately withheld his 2023 conviction.

Key holding: Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) precludes reliance on the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt, but does not preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

Sections 85ZR and 85ZS are directed to the fact of a charge, conviction or finding of guilt and do not expressly preclude an administrative decision-maker from considering the underlying conduct.

entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2505
entry.content:
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2501
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Harvey v State of Queensland [2026] QCA 214
entry.content:
The Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Harvey’s appeal from a decision refusing to set aside his notice of discontinuance of a police assault damages claim filed more than seven years earlier. The Court found no error in the primary judge’s discretionary conclusion that the appellant had not shown good reason, or that the interests of justice required, setting aside the discontinuance, given unparticularised evidence and unexplained delay.

Key holding: Even if a court may set aside a notice of discontinuance where the interests of justice require it, unparticularised claims of duress or mental illness and lengthy unexplained delay will not satisfy that test.

Assuming in the appellant's favour that the court had power to set aside the discontinuance if it was shown to be in the interests of justice to do so, the material before the primary judge did not satisfy that test.

entry.title: ZCGS and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2499
entry.content:
ZCGS sought merits review of a 2019 protection visa refusal under s 36(1C) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), having earlier withdrawn an AAT review of the same decision. The Tribunal held it had no jurisdiction to entertain the second application because the earlier withdrawal was taken to be a dismissal and a later application was barred. The application was dismissed under s 97 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth).

Key holding: Where an applicant withdraws a merits review application and it is taken to have been dismissed, the Tribunal lacks a reviewable decision for a later application concerning the same decision.

In the Tribunal's view, the effect of the Applicant having withdrawn his first application had the effect that it was taken to have been dismissed.

entry.title: Kola v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1550
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Mr Kola’s challenge to an Administrative Review Tribunal decision affirming refusal of citizenship by conferral under s 21(2)(h) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth). The Court upheld the Tribunal’s finding that his criminal history outweighed remorse, rehabilitation evidence and a low risk of reoffending.

Key holding: A low risk of future offending does not by itself establish that a person is presently of good character under s 21(2)(h).

An assessment that a person presents a low risk of future offending is not equivalent to a conclusion that the person is presently of good character within the meaning of s 21(2)(h).

entry.title: Brown and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2438
entry.content:

The Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed the reviewable decision, finding the disability and early intervention requirements were not satisfied. The case is a routine merits review of access criteria under the NDIS Act.

Key holding: For s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act, substantially reduced functional capacity is assessed by reference to what a person can do, not what they choose or are willing to do.

There is a distinction between a person's capacity to do a task as opposed to a person's willingness to do a task.

entry.title: Darlington-Thomas v Elgas Limited [2026] FCA 1566
entry.content:
The Federal Court granted Ms Darlington-Thomas leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth) to proceed against her labour hire employer, Zoom, for alleged disability discrimination. The AHRC had terminated her complaint against Zoom, but the Court held the claim was reasonably arguable and should be resolved with the overlapping claim against Elgas.

Key holding: On an application for leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act, the Court asks only whether the proposed discrimination claim is reasonably arguable and not fanciful, rather than determining the merits.

I am satisfied that the text, context and purpose of the leave requirement in s 46PO(3A) suggests that it is appropriate for the Court to consider in determining whether to grant leave whether the claims made by an applicant are reasonably arguable, and are - at the least - not fanciful. This is consistent with the language used in s 46P(1A).

entry.title: Gates-Pilcher and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2500
entry.content:
This case concerned an application for Australian citizenship by descent by a New Zealand citizen with serious violent offending and non-disclosure of his criminal record. The Tribunal was not positively satisfied that he met the good character criterion and affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: For citizenship by descent under s 16(2)(c) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the Tribunal must be positively satisfied that the applicant is of good character at the time of decision; if not, the application cannot be approved.

The Tribunal notes that the good character test does not require it to form an adverse view of the Applicant's character. Rather, it must be positively persuaded or positively satisfied that the Applicant is of good character.

entry.title: Gibson and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2437
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused an application to appoint NDIS participant Shannon Gibson’s support coordinator, Geeta Carroll, as his litigation supporter in a Tribunal review about his NDIS plan. Although the Tribunal accepted that Mr Gibson lacked decision-making ability, it was not satisfied that the appointment was “necessary” because his representative, plan-nominee mother, interpreter, Tribunal adjustments and informal supports already allowed participation.

Key holding: Under s 67(1)(b) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), a litigation supporter is not “necessary” merely because appointment is desirable, expedient, convenient or preferable; it is a last-resort measure required only where available and suitable other measures do not allow the party to participate.

It follows that the use of the word necessary has the effect that an appointment that would make the proceeding easier or more convenient to manage, or that the parties would welcome, is not for that reason 'necessary'. The choice of the word emphasises that an appointment is a measure of last resort, made only where the party cannot otherwise participate.

Key holding: Under s 34(1) of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), all criteria are cumulative, so if any criterion is not met the support is not reasonable and necessary and cannot be funded in a statement of participant supports.

entry.title: Baraboutis and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2417
entry.content:
Ms Baraboutis sought review of a decision refusing her access to the NDIS. The Tribunal accepted she had physical and neurological impairments and that some were permanent, but was not satisfied they caused substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act. It affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: In assessing whether impairments result in substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c), the Tribunal must consider each specified activity as a whole rather than by reference to isolated tasks.

Further, the requirement to consider an activity as a whole, rather than by reference to tasks considered in isolation (as made plain in the amendment to s 24(1)(c)) reflects the reasoning of the Full Court of the Federal Court in National Disability Insurance Agency v Foster (2023) 295 FCR 521; [2023] FCAFC 11 ('Foster').

entry.title: Lippl and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2416
entry.content:
This NDIS review concerned whether Ms Lippl should receive additional 1:1 support worker hours beyond those in her statement of participant supports. The Tribunal was not satisfied the requested additional hours represented value for money, finding her current flexible supports sufficient and an increase risked dependency. It nonetheless set aside and remitted the matter to fix the SoPS wording and specify support-worker assistance in accordance with the orders.

Key holding: Additional requested NDIS support worker hours are not reasonable and necessary where the evidence shows the participant can use current flexible funding to meet needs and increased hours risk dependency, so the value-for-money criterion is not met.

The Tribunal has determined the requested additional support worker hours do not satisfy the statutory requirement of representing value for money and cannot be approved by the Tribunal. The evidence is that Ms Lippl can use her support worker hours flexibly, that the current provision is sufficient to meet her needs and that increasing her hours risks creating dependency on support workers over time.

entry.title: BNE24 v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1561
entry.content:
This was an appeal from the Federal Circuit and Family Court (Division 2) dismissing review of a Tribunal decision refusing a protection visa. The unrepresented appellant argued the Tribunal’s adverse credibility findings were illogical or unreasonable. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal, holding the primary judge correctly found no jurisdictional error.

Key holding: A Tribunal’s adverse credibility finding does not involve jurisdictional error merely because a reviewing court would have reached a different factual finding; the reasoning must be legally unreasonable.

Therefore, jurisdictional error in the reasoning by the Tribunal as to the credibility of the account given by an applicant is not established by seeking to persuade a court on review that the Tribunal's reasoning includes an error in the sense that the Court would not make the same finding.

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

Key holding: In South Australia, s 9(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act 2016 (SA) (and by parity s 12(1)) is a law relating to evidence picked up by s 79(1) of the Judiciary Act and applies in federal family law proceedings, so a recording obtained for a lawful-interest purpose cannot be used unless a s 9(1) exception applies, and s 138 of the Evidence Act does not displace that prohibition.

In my view, subsection 9(1) is therefore a "law relating to evidence," the effect of which is that it is "picked up" by section 79 of the Judiciary Act[17] such that the same limitation applies in the context of a court exercising federal jurisdiction in South Australia, as is the case in the present proceeding. The same reasoning applies with respect to subsection 12(1) of the Surveillance Devices Act.

Key holding: Where a non-citizen fails the character test after mandatory visa cancellation, the Tribunal may revoke cancellation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii) if satisfied there is another reason, exercising the discretion in accordance with the applicable ministerial direction.

Section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act requires the Tribunal to consider if there is another reason why the discretion should be exercised to revoke the original decision. In exercising this discretion, the Tribunal must have regard to the Direction (s 499(2A)).

entry.title: Hares (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2454
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to grant Subclass 309 (Spouse (Provisional)) visas to Mr Mohamad Bali and family, sponsored by Ms Bassima Hares. The Tribunal had to decide whether the couple was in a genuine and continuing married relationship under s 5F of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) at application and at decision. It affirmed the refusal because, despite accepting a valid marriage, it was not satisfied on the evidence of mutual commitment, a joint household or a genuine continuing relationship.

Key holding: Abundant documentary evidence alone does not establish a genuine spousal relationship; the Tribunal must be positively satisfied of the s 5F(2) elements on all the circumstances.

Documentary evidence in itself, no matter how abundant, does not establish in the Tribunal's view the existence of a genuine spousal relationship.

entry.title: Gunarathne (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2449
entry.content:
This was a review of a refusal to grant a New Zealand Citizen Family Relationship (Temporary) (Class UP) Subclass 461 visa. The applicant applied while holding only a Bridging A visa and failed to satisfy the Schedule 3 criteria required because he did not hold a substantive visa. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: Failure to satisfy either of the cumulative requirements in Schedule 3 criterion 3004(d) or 3004(f) prevents an applicant from meeting criterion 3004 as a whole and therefore cl 461.213(b)(ii).

As I am not satisfied the applicant meets 3004(d) or (f), it follows that the applicant does not meet 3004 as a whole. Accordingly, he does not satisfy cl 461.213(b)(ii) of Schedule 2 to the Regulations and cannot meet the requirements for the grant of the visa.

entry.title: 2306518 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2406
entry.content:
In 2306518 (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2406, the Tribunal reviewed a refusal of a Partner (Temporary) (Class UK) visa (Subclass 820) after the applicant’s relationship with his sponsor ceased. The applicant claimed to have experienced family violence, but the Tribunal was not satisfied and obtained an Independent Expert opinion that he had not. Because the opinion was validly made, the Tribunal treated it as correct and affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: Where a non-judicially determined family violence claim is referred to an Independent Expert and the opinion is validly made, the Tribunal must accept that opinion as correct and cannot prefer other reports.

I am required to take the opinion of the Independent Expert as correct, unless that opinion is not validly made. The Tribunal cannot decide to give weight to other reports in the circumstances where the Tribunal has referred the matter to an Independent Expert.

entry.title: Triolo (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2358
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to grant a 95-year-old Italian citizen a Visitor (Class FA) visa, Subclass 600. The Tribunal had to decide whether the grant would authorise a stay of more than 12 consecutive months and, if so, whether exceptional circumstances existed under cl 600.215. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no exceptional circumstances and noting other visitor-visa criteria were also in issue.

Key holding: An intention or desire to remain permanently in Australia, even if reasonable and based on need for care and medical treatment, cannot be an exceptional circumstance for a further temporary visitor visa under cl 600.215.

I also consider that, where a person clearly desires and intends to stay permanently in Australia, (however reasonable and even where it is based on an applicant's need for care and medical treatment as in this case) that desire cannot reasonably be considered to be an exceptional circumstance for the grant of a further temporary visa.

entry.title: Majak and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2277
entry.content:
Majak sought review of a delegate’s decision not to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his Class XB Subclass 202 visa under s 501(3A) after serious assault convictions. The Tribunal accepted he failed the character test but found “another reason” to revoke under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii), principally the best interests of his infant daughter and the extreme impediments if removed to South Sudan. It set aside the delegate’s decision and substituted revocation.

Key holding: Where the Tribunal is satisfied on the evidence that another reason exists, it should set aside the non-revocation decision and substitute revocation under s 501CA(4)(b)(ii).

Having reached this conclusion, I find that there is 'another reason' for the revocation of the cancellation decision for the purposes of section 501CA(4)(b)(ii) of the Act. Accordingly, it is appropriate for me to set aside the decision under review and substitute decision that the cancellation decision be revoked.
